title: Tax Office reminds crypto holders: you still need to declare it, even if the exchange is overseas
excerpt: The Tax Office says it now has the data to check 1.4 million crypto accounts. If you bought, sold, or earned crypto this year, you need to put it on your tax return.
body:
The Australian Taxation Office (the Tax Office) has put out a reminder that crypto, including Bitcoin, Ethereum, and other digital coins, is treated like any other investment for tax purposes. That means if you bought, sold, swapped, earned, or used crypto to pay for something, you need to declare it on your tax return.

The reminder comes as the Tax Office expands its data-sharing with crypto exchanges. The Tax Office now gets information from over 1.4 million accounts at Australian and overseas exchanges, under a new global standard called the Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework, which started on 1 July 2025.

Tax Office Assistant Commissioner Tim Loh said the Tax Office is now seeing "a complete picture" of what Australians hold in crypto, and that "the gap between what people report and what we can see has closed significantly".

Our take: this is the third year in a row that the Tax Office has stepped up its crypto checks. The technology is now good enough that even small wallets get flagged. If you have crypto and have not declared it in the past, the Tax Office is much more lenient with people who come forward voluntarily than with people they have to contact. If you are unsure whether you need to declare something, talk to a tax agent before you lodge your return, not after.
whatItMeans: If you bought and still hold crypto: You do not have to pay tax until you sell. But keep a record of what you paid in Australian dollars and the date you bought it. You will need this when you eventually sell.

If you sold, swapped, or spent crypto this year: Each of these is a taxable event. The difference between what you paid and what you received is a capital gain or loss, the profit or loss you made on the investment. You need to declare it on your tax return.

If you earned crypto as staking rewards (being paid to hold certain coins) or airdrops (free coins given to existing holders): These count as income at the value in Australian dollars on the day you received them, even if you did not sell them.
If your exchange is overseas: The Tax Office has the data anyway. Not declaring is the worst possible outcome. Penalties are typically 75 per cent of the tax you would have paid, plus interest.
